brief.head: The British way of war
brief.text: Every mil­i­tary builds on a pre­con­di­tion, Ajay Shah said. For Britain it was over­whelm­ing naval dom­i­na­tion; for NATO today it is air su­pe­ri­or­ity, which Russia never won over Ukraine. {029-C01}

brief.head: Hackers beat users
brief.text: Real ex­cel­lence, Ajay Shah ar­gued, comes from know­ing your tools well enough to take them apart and re­build them, as en­gi­neers did with the B-25 bomber. {029-C03}

brief.head: Drop, seize, hold on

lead.kicker: Varma and Shah pitch five stories for the screen
lead.head: Lights, camera, history

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 29

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah came with five sto­ries that, they ar­gued, should be films: three told by Shah and two by Varma, al­ter­nat­ing so that Shah went first and last. {#threetwo}
They had done a show like it be­fore. Pieces of his­tory like these, Shah said, could be a movie, should be a movie, and at worst were a great story that “gen­tle reader shall suf­fer from us”.
The can­vases were vast: the fall of France, the war in the Pacific, the birth of in­de­pen­dent India, the bat­tle for Kiev. Yet every pitch came back to one per­son fac­ing one prob­lem.

Varma put the prin­ci­ple in a sen­tence about his own story: “A macro­cosm of ide­o­log­i­cal zeal and one way of look­ing at the world com­ing to a fall can also con­tain the mi­cro­cosm of the re­la­tion­ship of these peo­ple.” {029-C07}
## Five pitches
Shah opened in the sum­mer of 1940, at the Algerian port of Mers-el-Kébir, where Churchill or­dered the Royal Navy to de­stroy the French fleet rather than let it fall to Germany.
Varma fol­lowed with a fic­tion laid over fact: ERP, an AT&T out­fit that preached clean cin­ema sound to the world, and a mar­ried cou­ple in­side it who begin to hear rooms dif­fer­ently.
Shah’s sec­ond pitch was the Doolittle Raid of April 1942, in which hacked American bombers flew off a car­rier, struck Japan and headed on for China.
Varma’s sec­ond was the mak­ing of in­de­pen­dent India, seen through VP Menon, the bu­reau­crat at Sardar Patel’s side, who as a school­boy had burned down his school.
Shah closed with the bat­tle of Kiev in 2022, and Volodymyr Zelensky, the co­me­dian pres­i­dent who would not leave.
## Why war makes cin­ema

Shah ad­mit­ted that some of his sto­ries are just things that blow up. But the Second World War, he said, holds the mind for a deeper rea­son: “Because the fate of the world is on the line. The stakes are sky high.” {029-C08}
The Falklands had dra­matic mo­ments, he said, but no­body wants that film: the stakes were so low, “like aca­demic pol­i­tics”. Varma held that any story with hu­mans in it has high stakes.
## No easy end­ings
Several pitches had no Hollywood res­o­lu­tion. Of Mers-el-Kébir, Varma said: “There is no vic­tory for any­one. There is a deep moral dilemma and a sense of un­ease and noth­ing is re­solved.”
Shah’s cau­tion against ver­dicts: “So hind­sight is easy. What’s re­ally, re­ally dif­fi­cult is stand­ing there.” {029-C02}

The same un­ease ran through Varma’s India. He loves the coun­try, he said, but feels deep dis­quiet that it was as­sem­bled from more than 500 princely states through co­er­cion and bro­ken prom­ises.
“The mo­ment you say that the end jus­ti­fies a means,” he said, “then you can make up any end in your head.” And then, he added, you can com­mit the great­est bru­tal­ity. {029-C09}
Small ac­ci­dents mat­tered too. A stranger’s ten ru­pees to a pen­ni­less young Menon, Varma sug­gested, may have changed the course of India.

The hosts closed with rec­om­men­da­tions. Varma chose David Byrne’s *How Music Works*, “the best book I’ve ever read about music”; Shah chose the YouTube chan­nel of William Spaniel, for some of the best un­der­stand­ing of the bat­tle of Kiev as it un­folded.

second.label: The princely states
second.head: Every dog accounted for
second.deck: Amit Varma on the Nawab of Junagadh’s flight to Karachi, and his priorities

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Nawab of Junagadh’s dogs

body: As India was being put to­gether after in­de­pen­dence, the Nawab of Junagadh re­alised he had to go. {029-S07} Amit Varma told what hap­pened next as a scene from a film.
A plane was char­tered. Into it went the trea­sury, the jew­ellery, his dogs, his be­gums and his chil­dren. As it was about to take off, one begum cried that her child was still in the palace.

The Nawab looked around and counted the dogs. All the dogs were there. “I love you, it was nice know­ing you. Please get off,” he told her, in Varma’s telling. She got off, and the plane left for Karachi. With 547 princely states, “or what­ever they were”, Varma said, there were 547 such sto­ries. {#stories}

quote.text: And he looks around, and he counts the dogs, and all the dogs are there

third.head: Ride a bike like a bat

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on learning to echolocate

body: What if, Ajay Shah asked Amit Varma, you could learn to echolo­cate like a bat? Varma asked if he was kid­ding. “I’m dead se­ri­ous,” Shah said.

Take peo­ple who lost their sight after about the age of five, once they had learnt to see. With care­ful train­ing, Shah said, two-thirds of them can ori­ent them­selves the way bats do, whistling and lis­ten­ing for the echoes. “This is the power that re­sides in­side each of us. We are just not aware of it.” {029-C05}
Some, he said, ride bi­cy­cles out­doors this way, sens­ing traf­fic and houses. {029-S03}

Varma brought a data point against, Thomas Nagel’s essay *What Is It Like to Be a Bat?*, and one in favour: a vis­ually im­paired col­league of Krish Ashok’s who lis­tens to ev­ery­thing at six times speed. {#sixx}

box.title: The rules of the pitch
box.text: Zoom in, Amit Varma said: a macro­cosm, like ERP’s zeal ris­ing and fall­ing, can con­tain a mi­cro­cosm, like a mar­riage. Ajay Shah’s test was the stakes: in­di­vid­ual life and death, with the fate of the world on the line. {029-C08}

sections.label: Pitch One
sections.head: Sinking a friend’s fleet
sections.caption: the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir
body: In the sum­mer of 1940, Ajay Shah said, Rommel’s tanks blasted through the Ardennes and France signed an armistice. What, then, of the French Navy, which by de­fault would fall into German hands?

For Britain that was in­tol­er­a­ble. In the British way of war, Shah said, the Royal Navy would al­ways have “a ridicu­lous level of dom­i­na­tion on the seas”, just as American and NATO doc­trine today be­gins with air su­pe­ri­or­ity. {029-C01}
Britain had landed some 300,000 men in France to fight along­side the French. {#expeditionary} Now it asked the French Navy, through in­for­mal chan­nels, to bring its ships over.
## Pride and obe­di­ence

Three things pulled the French the other way, Shah said: or­ders from Marshal Pétain’s Vichy regime, a mil­i­tary cul­ture of blind obe­di­ence, and a be­lief that France was a first-class power, even a Vishwaguru.
Some French of­fi­cers promised to scut­tle the ships if the Germans came for them. But that, Shah said, was a prom­ise about a fu­ture event.
At Mers-el-Kébir the Royal Navy pleaded until the very end. The French re­fused, Churchill gave the order, and about 1,300 sailors died. {029-S01}
Churchill wrote that it was one of the worst de­ci­sions he had to make in the war. Some his­to­ri­ans call it a mis­take; Shah sides with Churchill.
~ Amit Varma saw a film need­ing Hollywood scale with no Hollywood end­ing. Shah’s reply to the urge to judge was sim­ple: hind­sight is easy, stand­ing there is hard. {029-C02}

quote.text: So in that one de­ci­sion, Churchill cre­ated the death of thir­teen hun­dred French sol­diers who re­ally were not Nazi Germany.

sections.label: Pitch Two
sections.head: Hearing each other out
sections.caption: the couple who heard differently
body: Amit Varma’s first pitch was half fact, half fic­tion. The fact was ERP, the AT&T unit that preached clean sound to cin­e­mas across the world from 1926. The fic­tion was a mar­riage. His work­ing title: *Silence of the Heart*.
In his story a cou­ple join ERP to­gether, the way a cou­ple might join a re­li­gious cult or a physics lab. Part of their love is a shared pas­sion.

Then the woman starts to hear rooms dif­fer­ently from her hus­band and the other ERP men. At first, Varma said, she gaslights her­self: some­thing must be wrong with her ears. Later she owns it. Why is he right? Why is she wrong?
## A film for the ears

Everyone in a room hears it dif­fer­ently, Varma ar­gued, with­out being able to say so. “And in this hear­ing there is also a metaphor for the ways in which you see the world dif­fer­ently.” {029-C06}
Films often show cou­ples drift­ing apart be­cause they see the world dif­fer­ently, he said. He could not think of one about a cou­ple drift­ing apart be­cause they hear it dif­fer­ently. {029-S02}

~ Ajay Shah pro­posed a sep­a­rate fil­ter for each partner’s land­scape, “some­thing that is per­cep­ti­ble in Dolby Audio”. {#dolby} He called it a nice fem­i­nist film. Varma pre­ferred to call it a human story.

quote.text: But imag­ine two peo­ple drift­ing apart be­cause they hear the world dif­fer­ently.

sections.label: Pitch Three
sections.head: The plane nobody imagined
sections.caption: the hacked B-25 bomber
body: After Pearl Harbor, Ajay Shah said, America wanted to hit Japan it­self, to dis­rupt a for­mi­da­ble pro­duc­tion ma­chine and to punc­ture the com­pla­cency of a peo­ple fed pro­pa­ganda about their first strike.
Japan was out of reach. So en­gi­neers hacked the B-25 bomber in six­teen dif­fer­ent ways, adding de-icing gear and fuel tanks for per­haps 80 or 90 per cent more range. {#sixteen}
Shah drew a les­son for ev­ery­one: “You can be a dumb user of other people’s cre­ations, or you can know enough about them that you’re able to take it apart and mod­ify it”. {029-C03}
## A fail­ure of imag­i­na­tion

When a Japanese ship sighted the car­rier group and ra­dioed home, Japan pre­pared for a sea bat­tle. Nobody there could imag­ine bombers tak­ing off from a car­rier, hit­ting Japan and fly­ing on to China. {029-C04}
Amit Varma’s di­ag­no­sis: some­one was naval gaz­ing, not navel gaz­ing. “He was fight­ing the last war, so to speak,” said Shah. {029-J04}
~ Varma saw the film in its human mo­ments: crews told to take off early, not know­ing if they would come back, driven by duty, “even though your com­man­der is a guy called Doolittle.” {029-J03}

quote.text: But the in­ter­est­ing thing that hap­pened on the Japanese side was the fail­ure of imag­i­na­tion.

sections.label: Pitch Four
sections.head: Stitched, not discovered
sections.caption: the making of independent India
body: Amit Varma loves India, he said, and is glad he can go from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. But he feels deep dis­quiet about how it was put to­gether.

At in­de­pen­dence there were more than 500 princely states, 327 of them, he thought, re­ally small. {#princely} In two or three years Sardar Patel and VP Menon built them into today’s map, by means that in­cluded co­er­cion and bro­ken prom­ises.

Once you say the end jus­ti­fies the means, he ar­gued, you can make up any end and com­mit the great­est bru­tal­ity. {029-C09} He calls it fast-track coloni­sa­tion: what the British did over two or three hun­dred years, Patel and Menon did in a cou­ple of years.
Offstage, cats began scream­ing, “be­cause they get the sense of what I am say­ing”, he said. {029-J08}
## What if
Ajay Shah had his own coun­ter­fac­tu­als. What if India had not taken over Goa, now per­haps part of the European Union? {#goa} What if the British had kept Surat as India’s Hong Kong?

Varma imag­ined many small states, too weak to fight but com­pet­ing to gov­ern well. Shah doubted it: the princely states had very poor po­lit­i­cal de­vel­op­ment, with noth­ing like England’s path from the Magna Carta in 1215. {#magna}
~ The world is this way, Varma said, be­cause of a se­ries of ac­ci­dents. It could have been a mil­lion dif­fer­ent things.

quote.text: Imagine if there was a bit of a Hong Kong in India. What if the British had kept Surat?

sections.label: Pitch Five
sections.head: The comedian stays put
sections.caption: the battle of Kiev
body: In 2022, Ajay Shah said, the sup­pos­edly sec­ond most pow­er­ful army in the world smashed into Ukraine, a messy coun­try with weak in­sti­tu­tions. “Ukraine is like India,” he said.

Its pres­i­dent, Volodymyr Zelensky, was a tele­vi­sion co­me­dian who had once played the pres­i­dent of Ukraine in a show in which Russia in­vades. Many ex­pected him to flee, as Afghanistan’s lead­ers had.

He stayed, though early on there was an as­sas­si­na­tion at­tempt against him every day. {#assassination} He was no hero, he later said, only a man who knew that if he left, ev­ery­thing would col­lapse. {029-S08}
## Blind, but warned

Russian cy­ber­war­fare knocked out gov­ern­ment com­mu­ni­ca­tions, and of­fi­cials talked on WhatsApp. {#whatsapp} But Russians in­side Putin’s sys­tem had leaked the in­va­sion plans, and key de­fence as­sets were moved, so the first strikes hit empty sites.

Russian para­troop­ers took Hostomel air­port, as the CIA di­rec­tor Burns had fore­seen. Then the Ukrainians mounted a scrappy un­der­dog de­fence, even blow­ing up a bridge to flood a Russian route of at­tack. {#bridge}
~ The Russians with­drew from the Kiev re­gion. Amit Varma re­called Zelensky’s an­swer to an American offer to get him out: “I don’t want a ride, I want ammo.” {029-J13}

quote.text: Actually, I was just a scared, ter­ri­fied guy stand­ing in the gun sights, mak­ing a call every minute, every hour about what to do.
quote.who: Volodymyr Zelensky, in Ajay Shah’s telling

quote.text: And it strikes me that in this age we kinda have to do both. That you have both the first draft of his­tory and the sense mak­ing hap­pen­ing si­mul­ta­ne­ously.

p3.title: Now showing
p3.deck: Four tellings from the episode, and the lesson behind each

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on VP Menon’s origin story, in scattered scenes
stories.head: Cold lunch, then the matchbox
body: Amit Varma pitched it as a story told in scat­tered scenes. In the early 1900s a school­boy is failed in his ex­am­i­na­tion for poor at­ten­dance. He tries to ex­plain how far he has to come; the teacher will not hear it. He runs out in tears, grab­bing his lunch­box.

He sits shak­ing at a rail­way sta­tion where he likes to read. He walks by the river. Under a tree he eats his cold lunch and falls asleep as the light changes. He wakes at dusk be­side an empty liquor bot­tle some drunk­ard has left.
At a liquor shop he buys some­thing that looks like a bot­tle, say­ing his mother will pay later. Then he asks for a match­box. The last scene: the school is on fire.
The boy was VP Menon. He fled by train to Kolar, and decades later could still name every sta­tion on the way. {#stations}
In the Kolar mines he was soon giv­ing or­ders to men twice his age. {#mines} Then he sold tow­els on the streets of Bombay.

In Delhi he stepped off the train to find his pocket picked. A Sardarji stranger gave him ten ru­pees, a huge sum then, and Menon for­got to ask his name. “If that lit­tle event doesn’t hap­pen, India could be in a dif­fer­ent place,” Varma said. {029-S05}

~ Menon joined the gov­ern­ment as a clerk, nearly quit after the Rowlatt Act, and then de­cided that some peo­ple must stay within the sys­tem to change it. {#rowlatt} He be­came Sardar Patel’s ex­ecu­tor in bring­ing in the princely states.
stories.why: Behind the “ex­pres­sion­less bu­reau­crat” was a com­plex man, Varma said, for whom work was a mis­sion but who was bad with his wife and chil­dren. And be­hind the mak­ing of India lie tiny ac­ci­dents, like a stranger’s ten ru­pees. {#tenbucks}
stories.postscript: Varma’s source is Narayani Basu’s *VP Menon: The Unsung Architect of Modern India*. Basu, he thinks, is Menon’s grand­daugh­ter. {029-R05}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on VP Menon’s schoolboy fire

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the raid that shook Japan in April 1942
stories.head: Take off early, land nowhere
body: After Pearl Harbor, Ajay Shah said, America wanted to strike Japan it­self, though it was out of reach. The an­swer: B-25 bombers that could take off from a car­rier but not land on one. They would fly on to China, where Chiang Kai-shek’s Kuomintang pre­pared air­fields; Stalin had re­fused them Vladivostok be­cause of his peace treaty with Japan. {#vladivostok}

A Japanese ship sighted the group and ra­dioed home. The bombers took off early, from the wrong spot, hit their tar­gets with rea­son­able suc­cess and fell short of China. Most crews were res­cued by the Kuomintang. One plane landed at Vladivostok; the NKVD later staged its crew’s es­cape to Iran.
The raid came four months after Pearl Harbor, and it ended Japan’s sense of ease, Shah said. {029-S04}
~ Bystanders paid: Japan’s reprisal killed some 70,000 Chinese sol­diers and 250,000 civil­ians. {#reprisal}

quote.text: And sud­denly it changed the psy­cho­log­i­cal land­scape in Japan that we’re not get­ting away with this cheaply.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Doolittle Raid

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a prince, a pen and VP Menon’s nerve
stories.head: The pen was also a gun
body: Hanwant Singh, the Maharaja of Jodhpur, was being courted by Pakistan. “Jinnah of­fered me a blank cheque,” he told VP Menon and Mountbatten, in Amit Varma’s telling. {#jodhpurblank}
On paper, Varma said, the princes could join India or Pakistan or stay in­de­pen­dent. In prac­tice in­de­pen­dence was never pos­si­ble, and a state in­side India could not go to Pakistan.

They per­suaded him at last. Mountbatten left the room, and as Hanwant Singh was about to sign, he pointed his pen at Menon. The pen was also a gun. {#pengun} In Varma’s cin­e­matic imag­in­ing, Menon raises an eye­brow and smiles, and the Maharaja signs. {029-S06}
~ Years later Hanwant Singh of­fered to make Menon the MP from Jodhpur. Menon said no. {#jodhpurmp}
stories.why: India’s map was not drawn calmly. It was ne­go­ti­ated one prince at a time, with co­er­cion where needed and per­sua­sion where pos­si­ble, Varma said; and every princely state had a story like this one. {#stories}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Maharaja of Jodhpur’s pen-gun

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on AT&T’s crusade for clean cinema sound
stories.head: Crusaders against the echo
body: In 1926, Amit Varma said, AT&T set up Electrical Research Products Incorporated, ERP, to evan­ge­lise sound in cin­e­mas across the world. Its men car­ried kits, lis­tened for echoes and fixed rooms with pad­ding and drapes.

David Byrne, in *How Music Works*, pic­tures uni­formed men com­mu­ni­cat­ing through hand sig­nals and per­fect si­lence, “like some acous­tic Sherlock Holmes”. {029-J14} Yet in Canton, Ohio, they were baf­fled by a gen­tle roar near the screen, until they found six caged lions from a nearby cir­cus be­hind the stage. {#lions}
ERP went from about 1,000 screens at the start of 1929 to 4,000 by its end. {#screens} But the French burned a the­atre down, and India mas­tered sound and told ERP it was not needed. {#indians}
~ Onto this his­tory Varma laid a fic­tion: a hus­band and wife in ERP who begin to hear rooms dif­fer­ently. {029-S02}
stories.why: In France and India, Varma said, ERP’s cul­tural, al­most moral mis­sion met its match. It had set out to spread its val­ues ev­ery­where, “al­most like an American ver­sion of Macaulay”. {029-J15}
stories.postscript: ERP’s news­let­ter, Varma added, was called ERPigram.

quiz.q: What share of people who lost their sight after about age five can learn echolocation, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: About two-thirds; some even ride bi­cy­cles out­doors by whistling and lis­ten­ing.

quiz.q: Why did Japan fail to anticipate the Doolittle Raid after spotting the American carrier group?
quiz.a: A fail­ure of imag­i­na­tion: no­body thought a car­rier plane could reach Japan.

quiz.q: What did a Sardarji stranger give VP Menon at Delhi station, and what did Menon forget?
quiz.a: Ten ru­pees, a for­tune then; Menon for­got to ask the man’s name.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 29. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Winston Churchill (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Jimmy Doolittle (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (Government of India work, public domain).

shelf.title: How Music Works
shelf.creator: David Byrne
shelf.why: The best book Amit has read about music, which he gives to ev­ery­one: it shows how venues and tech­nol­ogy, from cathe­drals to CBGB’s, shaped the music played in them, feed­ing his ob­ses­sion with how form shapes the world.

shelf.title: William Spaniel (YouTube channel)
shelf.creator: William Spaniel
shelf.why: He had some of the best un­der­stand­ing of the bat­tle as it un­folded.

shelf.title: Wiring the World
shelf.creator: Emily Thompson
shelf.why: A fas­ci­nat­ing ac­count of ERP’s global sound cru­sade, in­clud­ing the French back­lash and how Indian film­mak­ers mas­tered sound and out­grew ERP.

shelf.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
shelf.creator: Thomas Nagel
shelf.why: Nagel’s essay ar­gu­ing that we can un­der­stand in­tel­lec­tu­ally how a bat nav­i­gates by echolo­ca­tion but can never imag­ine being one.

shelf.title: VP Menon: The Unsung Architect of Modern India
shelf.creator: Narayani Basu
shelf.why: A ‘mar­velous book’ that shows the dra­matic human story be­hind a seem­ingly ex­pres­sion­less bu­reau­crat.

shelf.title: India’s Greatest Civil Servant — Episode 167 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Narayani Basu

shelf.title: Integration of the Indian States
shelf.creator: VP Menon
shelf.why: A first-hand ac­count from the man who ex­e­cuted the in­te­gra­tion.

shelf.title: Nehru’s Letters — episode of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
shelf.why: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain on the clashes that shaped India’s early con­sti­tu­tional pol­i­tics: a ‘sleeper hit’ that shows Nehru and Patel re­spect­ing each other while dis­agree­ing, against both car­i­ca­tures of their re­la­tion­ship.

shelf.title: A Scientist in the Kitchen — Episode 204 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Krish Ashok
shelf.why: Krish Ashok on the sci­ence and ori­gins of Indian food, with the story of a blind col­league who lis­tens to audio at 6x speed, Amit’s favourite ex­am­ple of how much the brain can adapt.

shelf.title: A Bridge Too Far
shelf.creator: Cornelius Ryan
shelf.why: It im­mor­talises the failed Arnhem bridges op­er­a­tion, a bril­liant air­borne plan that col­lapsed be­cause the main forces never reached the para­troop­ers.

shelf.title: Servant of the People
shelf.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
shelf.why: The TV show in which Zelenskyy played Ukraine’s pres­i­dent be­fore be­com­ing it for real: the im­prob­a­ble start­ing point of the most un­likely ac­ci­den­tal-politician story.

shelf.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy playing the piano with, um, you know
shelf.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
shelf.why: A clip from Zelenskyy’s com­edy days that shows how im­prob­a­ble his jour­ney from co­me­dian to wartime leader was, and makes Amit’s point that mak­ing a fool of your­self on stage night after night takes courage too.

shelf.title: Dunkirk
shelf.creator: Christopher Nolan
shelf.why: Amit, no Nolan fan­boy, calls it the best war film ever made; Ajay, who knows the pe­riod deeply, sees it as the model for let­ting real events carry the drama.

shelf.title: Once in a Lifetime
shelf.creator: Talking Heads
shelf.why: It com­pletely blew him away and led him to decades of David Byrne’s music.

shelf.title: Talking Heads (YouTube channel)
shelf.creator: Talking Heads
shelf.why: The band that made Byrne, and Byrne’s ideas about music, mat­ter to him.

shelf.title: The Reformers — Episode 28 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films — Episode 23 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The first of the show’s se­ries of true sto­ries the hosts would turn into films, and Amit’s favourite episode at the time.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia — Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War — Episode 14 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

laughs.text: Amit’s mic kept mak­ing noises and flipped out of his kurta. Ajay told the cin­e­matog­ra­phers that ‘the struc­tural in­tegrity of his kurta is suspect’, which Amit called ‘such a mil­i­tary an­a­lyst phrase’. Admitting he wore the same kurta for the last sto­ry­telling episode, Amit gives a hint, ‘Grunge’, and chris­tens him­self ‘Kurta Cobain’.
On the Doolittle Raid crews obey­ing or­ders on a near-suicidal mis­sion: ‘even though your com­man­der is a guy called Doolittle.’
Amit on Japan’s mis­read­ing of the car­rier sight­ing: someone’s fatal sin was that he was naval gaz­ing and not navel gaz­ing. Ajay: ‘He was fight­ing the last war, so to speak.’

Ajay dis­misses the Falklands as low-stakes, ‘like aca­demic politics’, and Amit re­fuses to let the aside slip by un­no­ticed. Ajay fin­ishes it: ‘Why is aca­demic pol­i­tics so vi­cious? The an­swer is be­cause the stakes are so low.’
On Zelensky’s com­edy-to-presidency path, Amit: ‘the dif­fer­ence is that India did not make Kapil Sharma the pres­i­dent.’
While Amit voices his deep dis­quiet about how India was stitched to­gether, cats start scream­ing off­stage, ‘be­cause they get the sense of what I am say­ing.’

In a the­atre in Canton, Ohio, ERP’s acous­tic ex­perts were baf­fled by a mys­te­ri­ous roar and searched ev­ery­where for its source. It turned out to be six caged lions from a nearby cir­cus be­hind the stage. ERP’s news­let­ter, Amit adds, was called ERPigram.

Ajay asks the ‘mer­chan­dis­ing di­vi­sion of Amit Bhai Media Private Limited’ for a T-shirt read­ing ‘I don’t want a ride, I want am­mu­ni­tion.’ Amit: ‘Okay, the re­quest is in­stantly de­nied,’ adding that it’s for Ukrainians who love Zelensky to make it.
Zelensky’s leg­endary reply when the Americans of­fered to evac­u­ate him: ‘I don’t want a ride, I want ammo.’ It in­spired this episode’s fifth chap­ter title.
David Byrne in How Music Works imag­ines ERP’s en­gi­neers as uni­formed men com­mu­ni­cat­ing in si­lence, ‘like some acous­tic Sherlock Holmes’, able to sur­vey a room with their ears.

Amit likens ERP’s evan­ge­lis­ing of its sound val­ues to ‘an American ver­sion of Macaulay’, cul­tural im­pe­ri­al­ism through acous­tics. ERP ar­rived just be­fore Al Jolson’s The Jazz Singer ush­ered in sound cin­ema.
Trump’s ‘per­fect phone call’ with Zelensky, in which, per Ajay, Javelin anti-tank mis­siles were held up to pres­sure Zelensky into launch­ing a fake in­ves­ti­ga­tion against Biden’s son.
